coverage.label: Wednesday 4 November 2026, 0700 SGT → Thursday 5 November 2026, 0700 SGT

global.headline: DEMOCRATS TAKE BOTH CHAMBERS AND THE DOW HAS ITS BEST POST-MIDTERM DAY SINCE 1982
summary: The Associated Press called the House for the Democrats early on Wednesday, completing a sweep of Congress after the Senate fell overnight. The party flipped at least seven Republican Senate seats — Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas — with NBC projecting 54 to 44 and Alaska and Mississippi uncalled; CNN put the Democrats at a minimum of 240 House seats with more than 60 races unprojected. Hakeem Jeffries, on course to be the first Black speaker, claimed “a mandate for dramatic change” and Chuck Schumer promised “legislative razor wire”. Trump declined to take blame, saying “if I were on the ballot, we would have won” and that his rallies drew such love that candidates “weren’t able to transfer it”. Republicans told the BBC his focus on his legacy had cost them; Vance posted that “the reason we lost is the war”.

Markets read the result as certainty rather than risk. The Dow rose 1,569 points, or 3 per cent, to 53,356 — its biggest post-midterm one-day gain since 1982. The S&P 500 added 1.58 per cent and the Nasdaq 1.44 per cent, with AI-linked stocks lagging. Administration officials began preparing for oversight: committee control from January carries subpoena power, and Democrats have named investigations of the president and his family as an early priority.
global.geopolitical: Trump keeps the foreign-policy pen but loses the purse and the subpoena: from January every decision on Iran is taken opposite a chamber that can defund it or compel testimony about it, and allies from Ottawa to Jerusalem spent Wednesday recalculating what a two-year lame duck can deliver.
global.socioeconomic: The biggest post-midterm rally in 44 years was bought on the expectation that nothing large now passes — a wager against new spending and further tax cuts alike.

global.headline: TEHRAN READS THE VOTE AS ‘NO TO WAR’ AND BRENT GIVES UP THE WAR PREMIUM
summary: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, parliament speaker and Iran’s chief negotiator, posted that Americans had voted “NO TO WAR”, from conscience or from the cost of living, and that “we endorse this message” — adding that if Washington betrays that will, “our NO comes with a Nightmare”, and that the ball is in America’s court to prevent war. Trump rejected the reading: the war was necessary to stop Iran “having a nuclear weapon”, “I would have done nothing different”, and voters had backed the campaign while disliking that it “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term”. There is still no direct contact: the two-day window mediators set on Tuesday passed without a US answer to Mohsen Rezaei’s seven conditions for reopening Hormuz. The New York Times reported growing calls inside Iran for a nuclear weapon.

Brent settled at US$94.62, down US$8.98 or 8.7 per cent — its biggest one-day fall since April and its first close below US$100 since 7 October; WTI fell 8.3 per cent to US$88.12. Brent traded at US$118 on Friday and is down more than 14 per cent for the week; trend-following funds cut longs to about 55 per cent from 73 per cent in the session. Analysts called it a bet, not a deal: Rapidan’s Bob McNally said “Iran is hardened”.
global.geopolitical: Both capitals now claim the same electorate — Tehran as an instruction to end the war, Trump as a complaint about petrol — and only one of them must act before January, when the Congress that pays for the campaign changes hands.
global.socioeconomic: Nine dollars came off a barrel on a reading of an election, not a reopened strait: the relief reaches pumps and freight rates within weeks, and reverses on one incident in the Gulf.

global.headline: A DEAD POLICEMAN’S BODYCAM SHOWS THE KOMYSHUVAKHA SHELTER STRUCK AS THE TOLL REACHES 40
summary: Ukraine’s national police released footage from a camera worn by an officer killed at Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, on Monday. It shows residents moving towards an underground shelter after the first strike on the school, a radio warning of more glide bombs incoming, an officer shouting “Quickly, go to the shelter!” — then the shelter being hit and the recording ending. BBC Verify confirmed it was filmed where emergency services later recorded the aftermath. Police said a three-tonne FAB bomb hit the building, used as an aid distribution point, and that the second wave arrived as rescuers did, which is why the dead include police and rescue workers. Zelensky said at least 40 are confirmed dead and more than 30 unaccounted for, up from 33 a day earlier.
global.geopolitical: The second strike is the whole point: footage of rescuers being hit while responding moves this from a targeting failure to the pattern humanitarian law names, and it lands while Kyiv argues that Russian local truces are worth nothing.
global.socioeconomic: Aid distribution in the frontline belt now sets publicity against survival: a collection point has to be advertised to work, and being advertised is what the UN mission says exposed this one.

global.headline: HERZOG OPENS CONSULTATIONS WITH NEITHER NETANYAHU NOR EISENKOT HOLDING A MAJORITY
summary: President Isaac Herzog began consultations with party delegations on Wednesday, having accepted the certified results of the 27 October election, taking the smaller parties first and leaving Likud and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar until Thursday. Ynet counted 48 recommendations for Eisenkot to 46 for Netanyahu, with Ra’am backing Eisenkot and Yisrael Beytenu recommending him while ruling out reliance on Arab parties. Netanyahu argues Likud’s 27 seats, the largest single bloc, entitle him to the mandate; Eisenkot, Bennett and Liberman have all refused to serve under him, and his pardon request in his corruption trial sits inside Herzog’s calculation. Herzog warned that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled” if another election is to be avoided. The nominee has 28 days, extendable by 14. The election commission separately rejected Netanyahu’s claims of voting fraud.
global.geopolitical: The coalition arithmetic decides who negotiates a relationship Washington has already repriced — the US$3.8 billion-a-year aid memorandum is due to lapse on 31 December on Trump’s own announcement — and the midterms removed the congressional majority that might have blocked it.
global.socioeconomic: Weeks of bargaining with another election as the alternative keeps Israel on a caretaker footing, postponing every fiscal choice left by a year of war-level defence spending.

global.headline: THE COLD-STORAGE ATTACKS REACH FRANCE’S BLOOD SERVICE
summary: The Établissement français du sang said attackers reached the systems controlling cold rooms at three of its sites on Monday through one of its refrigeration suppliers, setting temperature and defrost thresholds to very high values. No blood products were lost, stock was moved as a precaution, and collection and hospital deliveries continued. ANSSI, the national cyber agency, and the health ministry are working with the EFS. Le Canard enchaîné named the supplier as Coolworld and reported room temperatures reaching 110C; the EFS confirmed neither. The campaign hit up to 700 French supermarkets in October and ten countries and British meat processors this week; it has now moved from food retail into the health system. Investigators keep finding the same weakness: operational-technology controllers reachable from the internet, in the French case with default passwords. Nobody has been attributed.
global.geopolitical: A fortnight of attacks on refrigeration has crossed from groceries into the blood supply with no state named: a capability demonstrated against a hospital input, and the only answer on offer is a contractor’s patch.
global.socioeconomic: The exposed asset was not the blood bank but its supplier’s remote-monitoring link, so every cold-chain operator now carries a vendor whose credentials are part of its own risk.

singapore.headline: THE CAT A COE PREMIUM HITS A RECORD S$139,001 AND PASSES THE BIGGER-CAR CATEGORY
summary: In the first November bidding exercise, which closed on Wednesday, the Category A premium for smaller and less powerful cars rose S$6,997, or 5.3 per cent, to S$139,001 — an all-time high, beating the S$133,009 set on 9 September, on 2,018 bids for 1,189 certificates. Category B rose S$433 to S$132,334 on 1,163 bids for 959 certificates, and the open Category E closed at S$135,998, so Cat A now costs more than both. Category C was S$92,000; motorcycle premiums fell a fourth consecutive round to S$10,689. The next exercise opens on 16 November.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is the example cities cite when they want to cap vehicle numbers by price rather than by queue, and an inversion in which the entry category outbids the luxury one is the part of the model that does not travel.
singapore.socioeconomic: The cheaper car now carries the dearer certificate, a day after the transport minister said the fleet cannot grow much further. Buyers shut out of Cat B are bidding inside Cat A — the distortion the proposed merger of the categories is meant to end, in a review not due until the first half of 2027.

singapore.headline: HDB LAUNCHES 7,964 FLATS IN THE FIRST EXERCISE UNDER THE HIGHER INCOME CEILINGS
summary: The Housing Board opened applications on Wednesday for 7,964 Build-To-Order flats across seven projects in Bedok, Geylang, Sembawang, Tengah, Toa Payoh and Yishun — three Standard, three Plus, one Prime. It is the first launch since household income ceilings were raised to S$16,000 for families and S$8,000 for singles. Prices start at about S$131,000 before grants, with four-room Standard flats around S$232,000 after grants, and waits of 34 to 45 months. More than one in three units are two-room Flexi flats, offered in all seven projects, against a target of 20,000 between 2026 and 2028. Applications close at 11.59pm on 11 November.
singapore.geopolitical: A state developer that sets both the ceiling and the queue is the counter-model to the mortgage subsidies most high-income cities use.
singapore.socioeconomic: Lifting the ceiling admits households that earned too much to queue without adding flats to this exercise: the relief is eligibility, the cost is longer odds for everyone already balloting. A two-room Flexi share above a third shows where the demographic weight now sits.

singapore.headline: THREE STATIONS OPEN ON 26 DECEMBER AND STITCH THE EAST INTO THE THOMSON-EAST COAST LINE
summary: Bedok South, Sungei Bedok and Xilin open for passenger service on 26 December, the Land Transport Authority said. Bedok South and Sungei Bedok complete Thomson-East Coast Line stage 5, Xilin extends Downtown Line 3, and Sungei Bedok becomes the interchange between them. Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said they join two major corridors and cut the Havelock to Changi Business Park journey from about 70 minutes with a bus transfer to roughly 45 without one, and that eastern residents will be able to ride the TEL into the city, north to Woodlands and — once the cross-border link to Bukit Chagar opens, now expected in February 2027 — into Johor.
singapore.geopolitical: The December opening pays off in February, when Woodlands North connects to Bukit Chagar: the east is being wired into a cross-border commute before that commute exists, which makes Singapore’s rail timetable part of Johor’s labour market.
singapore.socioeconomic: Twenty-five minutes off a daily cross-island trip, and one fewer transfer, changes where people take jobs rather than where they live, and it lands on the Bedok and Changi Business Park corridor first.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE LOOKS AT THE DOMAIN NAME SYSTEM TO IDENTIFY AI AGENTS, AND WEIGHS A NATIONAL REGISTRY
summary: Senior Minister of State Jasmin Lau told Parliament on Wednesday that the Infocomm Media Development Authority is working with GoDaddy, Infoblox, Cloudflare and Google on whether the domain name system — the internet’s address book — can be adapted to identify and verify AI agents across platforms and organisations. That work will feed a decision on whether further common infrastructure, including a national registry, is needed. She was answering an adjournment motion by Tin Pei Ling, who proposed a registry letting any party check an agent’s identity and mandate. GovTech is separately building a register of AI agents for about 150,000 public officers, recording who owns each and what it does.
singapore.geopolitical: Identity for autonomous software is being settled now: putting agent verification inside DNS uses infrastructure that is already global, rather than a national licence regime no one abroad would honour.
singapore.socioeconomic: The question Lau framed is who answers for an agent’s actions. Pinning each agent to an accountable owner is the precondition for letting agents transact at all, and the government is testing that on its own 150,000 officers first.

singapore.headline: SHANMUGAM AND FADLI FAWZI CLASH OVER A HOME TEAM MEETING WITH ISRAELI OFFICIALS
summary: In an 18-minute exchange in Parliament on Wednesday, Senior Minister K. Shanmugam rejected Workers’ Party MP Fadli Fawzi’s argument that Singapore should have raised West Bank settlements and settler violence, and restated their illegality under international law, at an operational meeting with Israeli officials. Shanmugam said the questions sought to cast the government as unprincipled and soft on Israel and read international relations through race and religion; Fadli rejected that characterisation. He asked whether the same principle would require raising Singapore’s concerns in operational talks with other Middle Eastern or Asian states. The questions follow a 7 September Haaretz report of a visit by a delegation including the Israel Prison Service, which claimed the death penalty was discussed — a claim Shanmugam calls categorically false and for which he said no public-interest ground was met for a POFMA correction direction, adding that he does not take Haaretz “very seriously”.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore’s practice is to keep working-level security contact separate from positions on conduct, stating the positions at the UN instead. The exchange tests whether that separation holds when the partner is Israel, two days after Washington said it would stop funding it.
singapore.socioeconomic: The argument was less about settlements than about who speaks for Malay-Muslim constituents on foreign policy, which is why a question about a prisons meeting was answered with a charge about race and religion.

word.definition: To redraw the boundaries of an electoral district so as to favour one party; the district so drawn.
word.etymology: Coined in Boston in 1812 from Elbridge Gerry, the Massachusetts governor who signed a redistricting bill, and salamander, the shape a newspaper cartoonist saw in the resulting district.
word.example: The cycle that opened with mid-decade redistricting closed with a Democrat taking a redrawn Californian seat from a long-serving Republican, a reminder that a gerrymander is a prediction and predictions can be wrong.
